newsitem.title: USA: IADB to gauge a decade of Latin American reforms.
newsitem.headline: IADB to gauge a decade of Latin American reforms.

text.p: The Inter-American Development Bank (IADB) will take stock this week of a decade of market-oriented reforms in Latin America, a region still beset by pervasive poverty and the world's most skewed income distribution.

Starting on Thursday, the IADB, which over the past few years has become the region's primary source of multilateral financing, will hold a series of seminars in Barcelona, Spain, ahead of its board of governors meeting next week.
The seminars will attract finance ministers from Latin America and the Caribbean as well as high-ranking officials from industrialized countries that are shareholders in the Washington-based IADB.
The bank hopes to send out a positive message to counter the sense of despair it notes in the region, despite a steady recovery from the "tequila effect" of the 1995 peso crisis.
"The current trends point to a renewed acceleration of growth. The prospects for 1997 and 1998 are strong," the IADB's chief economist, Ricardo Hausmann, told Reuters.

According to Hausmann, a former Venezuelan planning minister, regional GDP growth could top 4.5 percent this year, up from about 3.5 percent in 1996 and a dismal 0.8 percent in 1995, Latin America's worst performance so far this decade.
Nevertheless, the rebound is still too weak for a region where one out of three people live in poverty and tens of millions survive on incomes of less than one dollar a day.

In a seminar to be held on Sunday, officials and economists will analize the impact of economic volatility, growth and income disparity a decade after most Latin American countries embarked on programs of fiscal austerity and privatization.

Hausmann, who noted that performance has varied widely among early and late reformers, as well as how strictly they stuck to the plan, argued that the overall outcome should be more stable and sustainable growth.
"In general terms, this growth cycle seems to be led by an increase in exports and investment rather than by one-time economic adjustments," he said.

Other macroeconomic indicators bode well for Latin America. Fiscal discipline has continued to improve, leading to an 11 percent regional inflation, the lowest since 1977, and shrinking budget deficits in many countries.

The IADB has also preached that sobriety in public sectors once hooked on deficit spending must be bolstered by investment in human capital, namely providing better education and health services to their populations.

In that sense Latin America's problem is not a lack of funds but of efficiency. The region devotes a larger portion of its resources to social programs than East Asia, but its results are markedly poorer.
Latin Americans on average have two years less schooling than their East Asian counterparts, largely due to a system that has long favored vote-garnishing public universities over basic education.

In coming years, those that stay on the straight and narrow should see poverty and unemployment rates pushed up by privatization start to fall as in Chile, a country often cited as an example of a successful transition to a market economy.
Experiences in other countries have varied, although most followed a boom-and-bust pattern after a first round of reforms.
Argentina and Mexico, the worst hit by the "tequila effect," rebounded strongly but are burdened with naggingly high unemployment and face electoral pressures this year.
Countries like Bolivia have plodded ahead with reforms for more than a decade but have yet to strike out at poverty.

According to a recent World Bank study, crime and violence have stunted economic growth in Latin America. In Colombia, which suffers the world's highest murder rate, they robbed it of some 10 percentage points of GDP over the past two decades.
